rows.claim: a tools/call carrying no `params.name` emits NO `mcp-name` header, rather than an empty one
rows.evidence: routing_headers_test.exs:193-200 — the send is `"method" => "tools/call"` with `"params" => %{}`, and routing_headers_test.exs:200 asserts `refute Map.has_key?(headers_of(agent, 0), "mcp-name")`. The axis's SUBJECT is exactly this header's presence on a tools/call, so match-relation.md §6's mention-is-not-a-discharge rule does NOT make this silent — the two are about the same behaviour and they disagree. The check is not conditional on the field existing: the addressed `dispatch_site` excerpt shows `handlePost` calling `this.checkMcpNameHeader(e,n,`params.name`)` on every tools/call, and with no `params.name` the predicate binds `i` and `a` undefined, takes the falsy arm and pushes `Missing Mcp-Name header on ${r} request. Clients MUST include the Mcp-Name header for ${r} requests.` — i.e. FAILURE. So a client doing what this member asserts would be scored FAILURE by this check on this input. It runs green only because the scenario's fixture never sends a nameless tools/call. The match axis is silent: with no source field there is nothing to match.

rows.claim: a non-ASCII tool name rides `mcp-name` as the Base64 sentinel and decodes back to the body value
rows.evidence: routing_headers_test.exs:211 binds `name = "天気_get"`; routing_headers_test.exs:222 asserts `assert String.starts_with?(header, "=?base64?")` and routing_headers_test.exs:223 asserts `assert HeaderMirror.decode_value(header) == name`, with routing_headers_test.exs:226 confirming the BODY still carries the plain name. Presence agrees: routing_headers_test.exs:222's subject is a property OF the header's value, which a missing header could not satisfy. The MATCH axis contradicts: the check's `a!==i` is a raw string comparison of the header against `t.params?.name`, and nothing on the client leg's `mcp-name` path decodes the sentinel — the only `=?base64?` handling in the build is SERVER-leg (`sep-2243-server-decode-base64` and siblings, a different scenario, measured by search over the build's seven occurrences of that literal). So the encoded header is not `===` the plain body name and the check pushes a mismatch error. A conformant client — streamable-http.mdx requires the encoding — is scored FAILURE here; it runs green only because the fixture's tool names are plain ASCII.

rows.claim: a CRLF-bearing tool name is neutralised — it rides `mcp-name` encoded, carries no raw CR, and injects no header
rows.evidence: routing_headers_test.exs:250 binds the hostile name; routing_headers_test.exs:261 asserts `assert HeaderMirror.decode_value(headers["mcp-name"]) == hostile`, routing_headers_test.exs:262 asserts `refute headers["mcp-name"] =~ "\r"` and routing_headers_test.exs:263 asserts `refute Map.has_key?(headers, "x-injected")`. Presence agrees — routing_headers_test.exs:261's assertion decodes the header's value. The match axis contradicts for the same reason as the non-ASCII row: the check compares the RAW header against `t.params?.name` with `a!==i`, and the encoded form is not the hostile literal. Here the disagreement has a security shape: satisfying the check literally would mean putting a CRLF-bearing value on the wire unencoded.

rows.claim: `encode!/1` returns the JSON string bare rather than wrapped in an `{:ok, _}` tuple
rows.escalation: no_axis_contact — every axis of this check is silent. A3 §2 rules that covering zero of one axis is no match, not a partial one; generalised to 1 axes that is this edge. §3's table has no row for it, so it escalates rather than being bucketed.
rows.evidence: protocol_test.exs:182-185 — `json = Protocol.encode!(request)`, then `assert is_binary(json)` and `assert Jason.decode!(json)["method"] == "ping"`. The subject is the BANG VARIANT'S RETURN TYPE: that encode!/1 hands back the binary its non-bang sibling wraps in a tuple. The second assert reads one field to show the binary is the right message, which is a sanity check on the test rather than a claim about wire validity — and how_a_silent_axis_was_decided is conservative by rule, so an incidental assertion is not coverage.
rows.note: ALL AXES SILENT, so this escalates as `no_axis_contact` and is not bucketed. Dropping the edge instead would make the member look edge-less and therefore bucket 1, which asserts `we looked and there is no counterpart` — false here: the counterpart is WireSchemaValid, the same check its two siblings above match, and what is true is that this claim does not touch its predicate. That is the distinction `the_all_silent_case` was written for, and this is its fifth instance.
oc_key: Every JSON-RPC message the implementation sent is valid per the spec JSON schema for the negotiated spec version

rows.claim: a request whose _meta names a real but unsupported earlier version is rejected with -32022
rows.escalation: no_axis_contact — every axis of this check is silent. A3 §2 rules that covering zero of one axis is no match, not a partial one; generalised to 3 axes that is this edge. §3's table has no row for it, so it escalates rather than being bucketed.
rows.evidence: dispatch_test.exs:109-112 — `assert resp["error"]["code"] == -32_022` for `_meta` carrying `"2025-11-25"`. The assertion's subject is the error CODE; all three of the check's axes are predicates on `error.data` — that it carries a non-empty `supported` array, that every entry is a version the server reports, and that `requested` echoes what was asked for. Nothing in this unit reads the error object's data member at all.
rows.note: ALL AXES SILENT, escalated as `no_axis_contact`, never bucketed. This is the client-leg file's `the_all_silent_case` on the server leg, and it is a finding rather than an accident: the OC check scores the SHAPE of the UnsupportedProtocolVersionError's data and this SDK's suite scores only its code. The check is RED at the accepted run, so the silence is not harmless — it is the precise reason our green tells us nothing about why the harness failed us here.
oc_key: If the server does not implement the requested version (whether the version is unknown to the server, or is a known version the server has chosen not to support), it MUST respond with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError listing the versions it does support; the error data carries the supported versions and echoes the requested version.

rows.claim: validate_protocol_version/2 classifies a known earlier version as unsupported, echoing the version it was given
rows.escalation: no_axis_contact — every axis of this check is silent. A3 §2 rules that covering zero of one axis is no match, not a partial one; generalised to 3 axes that is this edge. §3's table has no row for it, so it escalates rather than being bucketed.
rows.evidence: meta_test.exs:50-51 — `assert Meta.validate_protocol_version(meta, @version) == {:error, {:unsupported, "2025-11-25"}}`. The tuple DOES carry the requested version back, which is the nearest this unit comes to the `error_data_requested_echoes_the_requested_version` axis — and it is not near enough. The axis is a predicate on `error.data.requested`, a WIRE field of the JSON-RPC error object; `{:error, {:unsupported, _}}` is an SDK-invented container that B2b's own register records as `mixed` for that reason, and no assertion here follows it to the wire.
rows.note: ALL AXES SILENT, escalated as `no_axis_contact`. Recorded rather than dropped because the near-agreement is the interesting part: the SDK has the value the check wants and this unit stops one step short of asserting where it ends up.
oc_key: If the server does not implement the requested version (whether the version is unknown to the server, or is a known version the server has chosen not to support), it MUST respond with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError listing the versions it does support; the error data carries the supported versions and echoes the requested version.

rows.note: ALL AXES SILENT, escalated as `no_axis_contact`. Filed as an EDGE rather than as bucket 1 because the check's subject really is this member's subject — `DiscoverCapabilitiesMatchHandlers` is the capability-honesty rule and this unit is the capability-honesty test — and the mismatch is one of GRANULARITY: the OC check scores honesty at the level of a whole capability (`tools`, present or absent, against `tools/list`), and this unit scores it at the level of a SUB-KEY (`tools.listChanged`, absent rather than false, against whether a delivery channel exists). A server could pass the check while advertising a `listChanged` it cannot honour, which is the gap the member was written for. Recording it as bucket 1 would say the suite has nothing on capability honesty, and it has; recording an agreement would say this unit corroborates a check it never exercises.
oc_key: capabilities matches what the server honors on real RPC calls

title: escalated — routed to the PM, in NO bucket
what_this_is: THE ELEVENTH VIEW, OUTSIDE THE TEN. The crosswalk's own rule is that "an escalation is NOT a bucket and is never counted as one" (match-relation.md §7). These rows are therefore visibly excluded by rule, each with its reason, rather than invisibly dropped — and rendering one into a bucket would launder a PM escalation into an adjudication, which is the one thing this ticket must not do. AC2's partition holds over the 93 BUCKETED edges; these 13 are enumerated here and are counted in the edge equation as their own term.
